item.title: Flow, In Depth
item.description:
Awe

Flow, In Depth

One way to channel a flow state is to stop trying and just be.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • A flow state entails alignment of goals, energy, attention, feedback, and so on.
  • When we learn what we can control in our sport and direct our attention there, we make flow possible.
  • Flow is a pleasant experience. Athletes crave it. But there’s plenty in sport that’s unpleasant.
  • Opening what’s unpleasant and beyond our control can offer energy that’s deeper than flow.

Have you ever participated in something awesome? Awesome in the root sense of the word—full of awe—in which you gave of yourself as a participant or as a witness (or both), and in doing so, you allowed the boundaries of your conscious mind to dissolve as you connected with something greater: humanity, history, nature, or the divine?

In sport, this sort of experience is often discussed as flow, but the kind of flow I’m talking about transcends the field of play and/or the performance space, be it athletic, artistic, or otherwise.

Carl Jung called such experiences numinous, from the Latin numen, divine will. In a numinous experience, which might be delightful, terrifying, or both simultaneously, we surrender any efforts at control to something larger than ourselves. We let the divine, however you choose to conceive it, flow in.

Flow in sport performance literature (Csizkszentmihalyi, 1975/1990) has to do with performance and engagement. Flow is conceived of, in the literature, as a psychological state with measurable structural conditions: the balance between challenge and skill (sometimes depicted as an inverted U), clarity of goals and purpose, and action and awareness. Things are maximally ordered, and all is aligned: task, skill, focus, feedback, and so on.

The literature presents flow as something secular and comprehensible. And there’s good reason for this: those of us who support athletes—whether as researchers and scientists, as coaches, counselors, or service-providers—want to help athletes control what they can control, and we want to help athletes highlight what they do have control over so that they can put their focus there. This is what makes flow possible in the first place.

But when you witness an athlete truly in the current of a flow state—when you are an athlete allowing yourself to ride the current of a flow state—you’re a part of something sacred. There is soul. That soul is immeasurable. And it may not always be pretty or pleasant: it might be vast and fearsome.

In his later work, Csikszentmihalyi explored this vastness, writing about autotelic experiences—things done for their own reward rather than for money or status—and autotelic traits—qualities of people who worry less about what others think, allowing themselves instead to be driven by curiosity and awe.

Where flow is a well-operationalized performance concept with indices that seek to describe its contours and complexities, the numinous is more about meaning than performance, and about dissolution that may be unsightly.

There’s a lot of talk in sport and in the sport performance literature about resilience and grit. There’s less talk, at least in the sport performance literature, about terror, dread, and dissolution. And let’s be clear: terror, dread, and dissolution are not an efficient path to a podium (or an efficient path to any place).

But we do athletes a disservice when we point them, relentlessly, toward efficiency and alignment. (We do ourselves, as humans, a disservice when we point relentlessly toward efficiency and alignment!) Social media, mass media, and funding entities overwhelm athletes with massive demands for “narratives” that are readily digestible for a large audience.

Even if such narratives are linked to intrinsic values (“I love my sport, I love my teammates, I want to share this love”), when the demands are externally driven (e.g., express a need for “content” or a “statement”), there is a neurobiological cost that is distinct from that of an action a person chooses for themselves. The demand for narrative coherence on schedule and for external consumption spikes cortisol and can contribute to burnout.

Burnout is a kind of coming apart quite different from Jung’s numinous. Burnout is about depletion, and often depletion over time, whereas Jung’s numinous experience is more like a moment of awe. When we’re burnt out, those moments of awe may be harder to access: we’re looking down at our phones, or we’re accomplishing tasks, and in so doing, we miss the shooting star (or some other unsayable thing that transcends the language of the everyday).

So, if you’re headed back into your fall sport season with your training plan and your to-do lists, wonderful. But also—and write it into the plan, or don’t! — make space to play and space to be afraid. Find people (or other living creatures) who welcome your playfulness and who can witness your fear. You can have your goals and work to align attention and energy toward them, and you can feel the air on your skin, the breath in your body, and the vibration in the atmosphere that might be divine will.

item.title: How the Calendar App Beats College Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

How the Calendar App Beats College Anxiety

Smart scheduling habits can reduce student stress and boost success.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • College anxiety spikes when transitioning from low-choice high schools to high-choice university environments.
  • Centralize academics and social life into one Google Calendar to reduce cognitive load and student overwhelm.
  • Sync Canvas or Blackboard .ics feeds directly to Google Calendar to track all college assignments easily.
  • Block daytime hours for deep study and complete a 15-minute Sunday calendar review to prevent missed work.

Every semester, clients will describe feeling depressed, anxious, overwhelmed, and unmotivated. They've come back to school from a chill summer break with little need to attend to major friction points. But once they hit campus, it all comes rushing back, and within the first 30 days, they're drowning. There are several evidence-based levers college students can pull to improve their mental health and, maybe proactively, avoid this early semester slump. Working out (both resistance training and cardio), better sleep habits, healthier food choices (eg. something approximating the Mediterranean Diet), and reducing alcohol/drugs/porn/sports betting are fantastic, proven tools that make our brains and bodies so much better.

But one of the most powerful, overlooked, and easiest to adopt is improving organization—more specifically, increasing the use of Google Calendar (or your online calendar of choice). College students often have their classes and assignments listed out on their Canvas or Blackboard. But how do they keep track of all of the other academic, social, and to-do list items that also require space in our brain and our day? They don't. They often rely on memory.

But not just memory, they rely on how they feel, too. So now we have a student who is trying to keep track of all of the moving parts of their life but also prioritizing things based on their emotional state and level of interest.

Why is this happening?

From kindergarten to 12th grade, school is in one building with a set start and end time. Friends, sports, and activities are all baked-in. There are fewer decisions and responsibilities—fewer moving parts to keep track of.

This is why I teach college students to use organization tools like calendar planning, not just as a form of anxiety reduction, helping their prefrontal cortex reduce the overload, but as a means of transitioning their brain from a low-choice (High School) to a high-choice environment (College). If it sounds kind of like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, separating thoughts, feelings, and choices, trust your instincts. It's one of the super practical tactics I share with students that has an incredible compounding effect without them realizing it's therapy cloaked as strategic planning.

Here are my go-to actionable steps for college students to get the most out of their calendars, decrease noise in their heads, and never miss something important. This is the list to send to your son or daughter.

Centralize: Make Google Calendar the single source of truth for all academic, social, and administrative obligations. I also recommend all appointments, travel, and even things like working out. One calendar to oversee everything.

Automate Canvas/Blackboard Integration: Extract the .ics calendar feed URL from the Canvas/Blackboard calendar tab and import it into Google Calendar via the "Add from URL" function.

Color-Code: Assign distinct colors to different feeds/categories (e.g., Red for Canvas, Blue for study/work periods, Gray for university admin deadlines).

Add a Little Description: No need to list out details of assignments or who's running a Frat meeting, just put enough info into the title of the block of time to provide orientation, making it easier to jump into whatever is on the next calendar item.

Sync the Official Academic Calendar: Download and subscribe to the university’s official academic .ics calendar to automate drop/add dates and university holidays. This lists not only when breaks are coming, but also Add-Drop deadlines, Finals week, etc.

Time for Heavy Loads: Do not just schedule classes; manually block 60-90 min blocks specifically for deep work or study sessions before 6:00pm. Heavy workloads are easier to start and finish during the day—less competition with the social scene and better brain functioning.

Give Every Hour a Home: Not literally every hour, but protect time on the calendar for fun stuff in the evenings, work blocks during the day, workouts, class time, etc. I highly recommend protecting daytime hours (like 9am-6pm) for class and work/study. After 6pm is for rec sports, hanging out, and general chill time. Homework at night is terrible (our brains do not function at nearly the same speed and quality).

Upcoming Week: Spend 15 minutes every Sunday night reviewing the upcoming week's synced deadlines to prevent blind spots. This small investment protects students from huge problems later in the week.

Share It: A college student's calendar can not only help reduce their anxiety and organize all of the moving parts of their life, it can help parents know what's happening, what's coming up, and how busy their son/daughter really is. It's vital that students share their calendars with their parents during their freshman and sophomore years. It's part of the process of building an adult human—we're transferring responsibility and oversight to them, but we still need a reasonable amount of transparency with their day-to-day.

item.title: Aging and Bipolar Disorder
item.description:
Bipolar Disorder

Aging and Bipolar Disorder

Personal Perspective: A soft landing after a hard bipolar life is possible.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Some research maintains that older adults can have serious consequences from bipolar disorder.
  • However, happiness usually dips in midlife and rises in the sixties and after.
  • Time allows bipolar individuals to recognize their cycles and triggers, and find treatment that works.
  • It is entirely possible for older adults with bipolar disorder to live a happy life.

A psychiatrist once told me when I was hospitalized for severe bipolar depression, “Bipolar disorder often gets better when you’re older.” I was about 40 years old when he told me this, and to this day, I curse myself for not asking him what he meant by “older:” 60s? 70s? Dead?

I decided to research the issue myself, but I couldn’t find an answer I trusted. As one study noted, “Little is known concerning the effects of aging on the manifestations of bipolar disorder.” Psychol Med, 2009 Apr 1;39(8):1247–1252. Another researcher concluded, “There is a paucity of evidence-based guidelines specific to OABD” (older age bipolar disorder, meaning over the age of 50). Curr Opin Psychiatry, 2023 Jul 17;36(5):397–404.

There are, however, some agreed-upon effects that come with advancing years: mania and hypomania tend to decrease, and depression becomes more predominant. Medication side effects can also be more difficult to manage in older adults. But the more studies I read, the more confused and irritated I got.

While admitting that definitive evidence doesn’t yet exist, some researchers have nonetheless maintained that older bipolar patients may face a host of horribles: decreased cognitive functioning, a decline in memory, an increase in physical ailments, even a shortened life span, among other things. But isn’t that the same chance everyone takes with age, I wondered. Growing older has serious mental and physical consequences for all of us.

A review of the pertinent literature acknowledged: “The clinical course of OABD is highly variable: the illness remains stable in some patients but seems to progress in others.” (Id.) So I looked at my own life and chose to believe what I have personally experienced: some aspects of my bipolar disorder have, in fact, improved with time. I believe there are advantages to aging that aren’t fully addressed in the research.

For example, mood patterns begin to emerge with age that aren’t necessarily apparent in the early years of a diagnosis. As you get older, you can begin to recognize the cycles specific to your own illness. In my case, it took many years for me to realize that I’m a rapid cycler—that my manic episodes usually last three days, followed by a four-day depression. Knowing this fact was critical not only to my treatment, but to my ability to cope with my symptoms. I knew they wouldn’t last forever—that all I had to do was hold on a few more days until my mood changed, as it almost always did.

Age also gives one the ability to recognize specific triggers and try to avoid them. With enough repetition, I’ve learned, for example, that financial matters in particular derail me. So I’m extra cautious around tax time each year—I’m careful to get enough sleep and minimize other stressors in my life if possible, and I’ve alerted my doctors and support team to keep an eagle eye on me until that time has passed. This heightened insight took many years to crystallize into action.

It can also take time to find the right mode of therapy (or therapist). One of my best coping tools these days is mindfulness meditation, which I didn’t even know existed until about ten years ago. I had to try countless types of treatment—cognitive behavioral therapy, EMDR, electroshock, biofeedback, gestalt therapy, etc.—before I finally found what worked for me.

And, of course, arriving at a proper medication regime often requires time-consuming trial and error. As anyone with bipolar disorder knows, most drugs don’t work right away, and experimentation with lots of different ones is more the rule than the exception. I look back on my thirties and forties as my guinea pig years; it wasn’t until I was in my fifties that my doctor and I finally found the ideal combination of meds to manage my illness. Time permits such tinkering.

This is not to say, of course, that bipolar disorder can’t be properly managed until one has reached a ripe old age. Some people get lucky and find a drug or a therapy that works for them right away. In addition, there is increased awareness about mental health these days, along with a growing decrease in stigma. Young people can surely benefit from this.

Nonetheless, it’s a well-known precept that happiness usually follows a U-shaped curve, dipping in midlife and rising again in the sixties and afterwards. Social Science & Medicine, 66(8):1733-1749. Despite losses and limitations, older people seem to have more equanimity. This may be partly due to the fact that the amygdala, the emotion-processing center of the brain, becomes less reactive to negative stimuli as we age. Psychological Science, 2004 Apr 15(4): 259–63.

In my case, age has brought a softening, a lessening of the harsh self-criticism I used to harbor. Fighting to regain my sanity over and over again has given me faith in my innate resilience. I don’t know if I’m wiser now that I’m older, but I’m certainly more resolute. I cling to life because I know that it is precious, and that every day I’m alive and well is an absolute victory.

I wish I could meet that doctor again, the one who reassured me that my illness would get better with time. I’d like to hear what he has to say about the conflicting research on this subject. But mostly I’d like to tell him that, in my opinion, he was right.

item.title: Stop Enabling Your Inner Critic
item.description:
Mindfulness

Stop Enabling Your Inner Critic

Your critical thoughts can't do anything. Only you can!

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Evolution gave us a survival brain that over-anticipates discomfort.
  • "Nexting" is Momentology's term for rigid, reactive, future-fixated thinking.
  • Though we can't eliminate our survival brain, we can learn to walk with it toward what matters.

Anyone remember this toy? "Weebles wobble, but they don't fall down" was the ad copy when these toys arrived on commercials in between Bugs Bunny episodes on Saturday mornings when I was a kid in Ohio. They are my metaphor for the Inner Critic, the inner "drill instructor" of the mind. Here's the thing about Weebles and our Inner Critic thought monsters — they have no arms and no legs! They can't actually do anything in the world!

Source: Photo by Mitch Abblett

Look how excited this little guy is, and yet he can't bang any actual drum. You'd have to do it for him.

In my Momentology approach, our inner Weeble is constantly yapping at us, leading us to leave the moments that matter and "next" our way into a future that hasn't happened yet. Instead of doing the bidding of our inner Weeble and leaving our moments due to the over-anticipated doom its yapping about, what if we ...
Listened without believing?
Looked at what's actually happening in and around us, including what matters and what fits the situation, the moment, we're in?
Leaped with action that only we (and not a weeble) can do: said the hard thing, made the tough decision, thought about how we might empower ourselves and others, let go of the clutter of a bad habit or a toxic relationship, or created something new?

I'm not saying your Weeble is going away anytime soon. The poor little guy is only trying to protect you (it's your evolved survival brain after all). He wobbles and yaps and may never fall down, but you will and he'll tell you a zillion reasons why you did. And you'll start up again believing that all the "nexting" he preaches will prevent it (but it doesn't).

Instead, let's help each other learn how to listen more to our moments, look with clarity, and leap with what fits and resonates. Let's see what the Weebles have to say about that!!

How does your Weeble wobble?

Try This: “360 Moment Scan”

You’re facing a tough situation, something that’s got your mind “wobbling” with anticipatory "nexting." Instead of scurrying around at the bidding of your inner Weeble, do these things instead:

1. Ask "What is my body saying right now?" Run your attention from head to toe and notice what it has to say by way of sensations and emotions.

2. Listen to the Inner Critic / Weeble’s yapping with a little “distance.” Notice how you can listen to the thoughts without having to do anything. Notice how you can look at how urgent they are, how blaming, shaming, and doom math-calculating they can be.

3. Look at the moment you’re in and ask: What is actually happening? What might I do that fits this moment and what matters to me?

4. Leap with an action that fits, that matters, regardless of the mind / Weeble’s ranting.

5. Notice the effects of having done so. Your mind (including the Weeble) and your body both get votes. So does what’s happening in the moment / the situation around you. Votes don’t equal verdicts.

Only you should be rendering those!

item.title: Are You Using the Wrong Measuring Stick?
item.description:
Cognition

Are You Using the Wrong Measuring Stick?

How to read the evidence of your life.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • A feeling can be real without our interpretation of it being right.
  • Discernment is perceptual literacy: learning not just to see, but to read what we see.
  • We can agree on facts and disagree on what the facts are facts about.
  • Judgment requires knowing the limits of the evidence.

In 1978, psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes described what they called the “impostor phenomenon.” They found high-achieving women sometimes feel they have somehow fooled everyone regarding their professional competence.

But imagine feeling this way before there was a name for it. You earned the degree, landed the job, and won the respect of colleagues. But you’re convinced that everyone will soon find out they misjudged you terribly. You’re really a fraud. Without another way to understand the experience, you are isolated. The feeling is yours alone. If you feel like a pretender so strongly, it must be true. Once the pattern is named and widely understood, however, there’s a chance this is just a distortion. Other people you admire feel this, too? Hmmmm, perhaps feeling fraudulent is not evidence of being fraudulent.

What Does a Feeling Prove?

A strain of popular psychological advice privileges trusting our intuition, listening to our bodies, and getting out of our heads. But the familiar false binary of head and heart can obscure something vital. Our lives are a dynamic improvisation of feeling and thinking. It’s always a yes-and. A thought can make your heart race. A racing heart can then seem to confirm the thought that produced it. Fear is real. Feeling fear does not necessarily mean you are in danger.

Discomfort is real. Feeling uncomfortable only establishes that you are uncomfortable. It does not yet establish what the discomfort means. I tell students that education requires the humility to admit we may be wrong or incomplete. We are not relaxing in beach chairs. We are doing intellectual labor. But how much thinking is enough?

Shakespeare gives us a useful gradient. Three young men in Hamlet are asked to avenge the violent deaths of their fathers. Hamlet indicts himself for “thinking too precisely on th’ event.” Laertes rushes ahead before thought can temper him. Fortinbras, though, finds something closer to the golden mean: he reads the circumstances, adjusts, and moves. At some point, thought must become action.

Learning to Read

This column has argued for a return to discernment: not simply collecting more information but seeing more. Seeing more of what? We can be accurate observers and still be undiscerning readers. Think about learning to read. Letters become syllables, words, phrases, meanings, implications, irony. The marks on the page are the same. What changes is what we can make of them. Expertise often works the same way.

A novice basketball player sees ten people moving around. A professional point guard reads the coverage, drop or switch, the low man, the nail digging, and the corner stunting.

Expertise is more than the continued accumulation of facts, moves, and calculations. Often, it means organizing what is visible into meaningful patterns. The novice sees movement. The expert reads the court. Discernment is perceptual literacy: the ability to recognize distinctions others may miss and determine which ones matter. It helps determine what critical thinking has to work with. Critical thinking analyzes and evaluates what we perceive. Discernment emphasizes the quality of the perception itself.

Wrong ruler. Wrong read.
Source: Photo by Dawid Matecki/Pexels

When We Ask Too Much of the Measuring Stick

Reading well also means knowing what our evidence can support. Consider routine bloodwork. If the numbers are all in the normal range, surely a person cannot have blood cancer. Except they can.

A standard CBC can reveal signs associated with many blood cancers. But some can exist without obvious abnormalities on the test. Every test has limits, though its boundaries may be known only to specialists. Physicians understand what any single diagnostic measure can and cannot establish and thus interpret lab findings within a broader clinical context.

Without that expert knowledge, we might assume every blood abnormality is being tested for. Why wouldn’t it be? The mistake is turning “nothing abnormal appeared in what we measured” into “nothing abnormal is there.” We have asked more of the measuring stick than it can deliver. We can make the same mistake in relationships.

Imagine a couple who have been fighting for months. Then the arguments stop. The house is quieter. One partner becomes easier to live with. Finally, things are getting better. We say, "The negativity is gone. We are therefore a healthy couple."

Probably, possibly, maybe.

Sometimes a relationship gets quieter because it is healing. Sometimes it gets quieter because someone has stopped trying. The observation may be perfectly accurate: We aren’t fighting anymore. The question is what that fact allows us to conclude. Silence can be peace. It can also be resignation. The facts aren’t false. They're just not dispositive. The picture may be incomplete. We may agree on the facts and disagree on what the facts are facts about.

Naming the Distinction

Discernment and critical thinking overlap, but discernment puts particular emphasis on what we notice before we begin testing it. Noticing the distinction comes first. Critical thinking puts it through its paces. And testing, in turn, refines our perception. Notice, test, refine, notice again.

It's possible to reason beautifully from a blurry picture. Discernment focuses what is available to reason. It asks us to perceive finer distinctions, understand what kind of evidence we have, and recognize when we ask our familiar measuring stick to tell us more than it can.

Refining perception should open possibilities, not prematurely close them. We can overread experience just as easily as we can underread it. A changed facial expression may be worth noticing. It does not mean we know what another person is thinking.

A skilled reader knows when a sentence permits more than one interpretation. Discernment requires the same balance of confidence and epistemic modesty. I can say this is my best reading now and understand that the interpretation is provisional.

Clance and Imes did more than give experience a name. They made a distinction available to others: a feeling that seemed privately true could be recognized as a common pattern and reconsidered. Discernment can do the same.

"I know I'm a fraud. Wait, this may be the impostor phenomenon."

"I know what this means. Wait, let me discern what the evidence actually supports."

So look again. Ask: What am I measuring? What does this evidence actually establish? What distinction might I be missing? These are the questions that advance our perceptual literacy.

The practice of discernment is a move toward higher fidelity. Less distortion, more wonder. Who's with me?

item.title: Eating Disorders Are About Eating but Also Much More
item.description:
Eating Disorders

Eating Disorders Are About Eating but Also Much More

What a eating-disorder diagnosis can and cannot provide.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • “Eating disorders aren’t really about eating” corrects one error but introduces a bigger one.
  • Restriction and bingeing generate psychological changes that can look like pre-existing traits.
  • Evidence does not support solving the “deeper” problem first and expecting eating to follow.

The patient is very knowledgeable about her condition and various treatment approaches. Among all the ‘facts’ she can rattle off, she says, “My therapist told me that eating disorders aren’t about eating.”

I have heard this phrase repeated so frequently about anorexia, bulimia, and other eating disorders; even among some professionals, it has achieved the status of clinical common sense: Eating disorders are not really about eating.

Admittedly, it sounds insightful. The danger is that it is also only partly true and, as in many other areas of life, half-true knowledge can sometimes be more dangerous than a false belief.

The aim of this statement is to correct a critical misconception: Eating disorders are not actually about making poor food choices or a lack of willpower. Empirical research and clinical observations show that people who suffer from these conditions typically have solid nutritional knowledge and strong willpower; they cannot simply decide to eat normally. Their struggles involve fear, perfectionism, self-perception, self-evaluation, self-regulation, emotion regulation, reward, habit, interpersonal experience, biological vulnerability, and, for some, trauma.

Anyone who has sat with a patient in the grip of one of these conditions knows that the food is never only food. But from there we tend to make a second mistake, and it is the more consequential one: We move from saying that an eating disorder is not only about eating to saying that eating is merely the surface expression of some deeper psychological problem. The food becomes a symptom screen. Underneath, we assume, hides the real disorder: trauma, low self-esteem, family conflict, personality disorders, and/or unmetabolized emotion (feelings that have not been fully processed).

I have to admit, it feels psychologically sophisticated. Scientifically, though, it is too simple and, hence, misleading.

Where a disorder lives is not why it started or how it was created

The main issue and misconception is not calling them eating disorders. The mistake is confusing the domain in which a disorder is expressed and maintained with a claim about what caused it: A disorder can be expressed through eating without having been caused by food. And eating behavior can become part of the machinery that keeps the disorder alive.

Let’s look at prolonged food restriction. Starvation does not simply make a person thinner. It also impacts and reshapes cognition, mood, attention, social behavior, reward processing, and preoccupation with, and rumination about, food. This is not uneducated speculation. The Minnesota Starvation Experiment, conducted by Ancel Keys and colleagues in the 1940s with 36 healthy male volunteers who had no history of disordered eating, produced depression, rigidity, irritability, social withdrawal, emotional lability, and an obsessive cognitive focus on food (Kalm & Semba, 2005).

The implication is challenging. Restriction can manufacture psychological features that we later read as evidence of a pre-existing personality problem. We meet the patient after the process has been running for months or years, and we mistake its products for its origins. That inference is plausible, but it goes further than the evidence settles: Recovered patients often perform much like acutely ill ones, and the unaffected sisters of patients show similar cognitive difficulties, which points toward trait as well as consequence (Holliday et al., 2005; Miles et al., 2020). Simply put, when you starve the brain, the brain behaves abnormally. We then look at that abnormal behavior and mistakenly say, “See, they were always like this.”

Bingeing can become self-sustaining in a parallel way. Eating may briefly reduce distress, shame, or emotional arousal, which makes the behavior more likely to recur. Purging and compulsive exercise can acquire similar reinforcing functions. This is the affect-regulation account, and it is contested: A meta-analysis of 36 momentary-assessment studies found negative affect rising before binge episodes but not reliably falling afterward (Haedt-Matt & Keel, 2011).

Once these cycles are established, whatever initially triggered the illness may no longer be sufficient to explain what is maintaining it. The disorder has become its own cause.

Why this is an important distinction at the bedside

If we believe eating is only the visible symptom of an underlying problem, a treatment sequence follows naturally: Uncover the deeper issue, resolve it, and normal eating will return.

Scientific evidence does not support that sequence.

In anorexia nervosa, nutritional rehabilitation is not something that can safely wait until the psychological work is finished. Restoring eating and reversing energy deprivation are themselves central components of treatment, not preconditions for the real therapy, and not a mechanical prelude to it. The American Psychiatric Association’s 2023 guidelines recommend that psychotherapy for adults with anorexia include normalizing eating, restoring weight, and addressing the psychological aspects of the illness together, rather than in sequence (Crone et al., 2023). A malnourished brain is not well positioned to do psychological work, which is part of why the order matters.

None of this diminishes the significance of trauma, relationships, identity, perfectionism, shame, or emotion regulation. For many patients these are profoundly important, and treatment that ignores them will fail in a different way.

It means something more precise: Causes, expressions, and maintaining mechanisms are three different things. What makes a person vulnerable may differ from what triggers the illness. What triggers it may differ again from what keeps it going. A model that collapses these into a single narrative will be wrong about at least two of them.

What a eating-disorder diagnosis can and cannot provide

Perhaps, then, we do not need to stop calling them eating disorders. The key is that we should stop using or hearing the name as an explanation.

Eating disorder tells us where an important part of the pathology occurs, and where a substantial part of the treatment must therefore go. It does not tell us why this particular person developed it.

That question is considerably harder.

If you or someone you know is struggling with an eating disorder, the National Alliance for Eating Disorders helpline offers free support. To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Against Medical Advice: The "Why" Behind Noncompliance
item.description:
Integrative Medicine

Against Medical Advice: The "Why" Behind Noncompliance

Patients knowing what they should do doesn't mean they can actually do it.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Having the right information is necessary for successful behavior change; however, it is rarely sufficient.
  • As humans, our choices occur within context, and each of us has a unique situation.
  • Understanding what stands in the way of following advice helps us understand the “why” behind noncompliance.
  • When healthcare teams work together, it changes the course of treatment and improves outcomes.

After the consultation and a battery of exams, the physician reached a diagnosis, prescribed the right medication, recommended a specific treatment, and sent the patient off with a set of pre-printed standard handouts. The patient’s condition, though, never improved as expected.

What happened? More times than not, the reason has little to do with the quality of the care being provided. Sometimes the prescription is never filled, or, when it is, the medication is not taken as prescribed or at all. When the recommendation is to exercise more or change eating habits, it may well be that the dietary change only lasts a week, and the exercise program never even starts.

In healthcare, the word for this is “noncompliance,” and although it accurately describes what happened, it does little to help us understand the most important aspect of the problem: “why” it is happening.

When the Irrational Makes Perfect Sense

Why would a person who just had a heart attack not take the medication that reduces the risk of another one happening? Why would a person with diabetes not change their diet as recommended and continue eating foods that make controlling their blood sugar levels next to impossible?

From the healthcare practitioner’s perspective, it seems completely irrational. From the patient’s standpoint, however, it might make perfect sense.

Let’s take the person who just had a heart attack. They go to the pharmacy to find the medication isn’t covered by insurance, and they can’t afford it, or they manage to get it, and the medication has side effects that interfere with work or intimacy. They may also be fearful of physical activity, believing that their increasing heart rate or shortness of breath is signaling another heart attack. Looking at the person with diabetes, the recommended diet may conflict with long-standing family traditions or require access to food that was out of reach for them, either financially or physically (i.e., food deserts). With many chronic health conditions, the psychological impact is often underestimated. Feelings of depression or frustration with the complications of living with a chronic disease, or simply feeling overwhelmed, can make even the simplest treatment plans seem like a hill too tall to climb.

We often fail to appreciate the distinction between our patients knowing what they should do and being able to actually do it. Having the right information is necessary for successful behavior change; however, it is rarely sufficient.

Knowledge in Context

It is widely known that it’s important to eat well, sleep well, and stay physically active. Yet, simply having that knowledge does not mean it always guides the choices we make. As humans, our choices occur within context, and each of us has a unique situation. The decisions we make are shaped by our unique contextual variables, and frequently those decisions are not aligned with what we know to be “best” for us.

article continues after advertisement

So, when a patient doesn’t follow medical advice or behave as prescribed, perhaps the right question isn’t:

“Why won’t this patient comply?”, but rather, “What contextual factors are getting in the way of this patient complying?”

This represents a small change in language with a big impact on how we understand patients.

A Treatment for the Person, Not the Symptom

Treatment plans for patients are typically aligned with evidence-based recommendations to improve a patient's health. However, those treatment plans don’t always align with the realities of the patient’s lived experience.

Let’s consider for a moment a patient with Type II diabetes with poorly controlled blood sugar levels. The response from a medical perspective seems straightforward: make medication adjustments, recommend nutritional improvements, increase physical activity, and continue to monitor blood glucose levels consistently.

These all seem reasonable and even easy to implement. But what if the patient is working two jobs, struggles to find healthy food options, cannot find time to go to the gym, and lives in a neighborhood that is not safe to walk in? The plan may not feel that straightforward. When the prescribed medication causes gastrointestinal side effects at work, and the patient has an elderly parent to care for after hours, resulting in only 5 hours of sleep per night, none of the recommendations feel “easy.”

Looking through this lens, the problem isn’t as simple as diabetes management. The problem becomes how to make diabetes management possible within this person’s life.

Integrated Health Revealing What Lies Beneath

This is where integrated health comes in. A physician working within an integrated care context can consult with or refer the patient to a psychologist who can help build understanding beyond whether treatment recommendations were followed. Exploring questions about illness beliefs, self-efficacy, personal and family psychological history, and emotions associated with the disease and treatment is relevant to better answer the question regarding what stands in the way of adherence. Once we understand that, collaborative solution-oriented planning can begin to improve outcomes.

article continues after advertisement

When we take the time to understand what stands in the way, we understand what lies beneath; we understand the “why” behind the noncompliance.

With that information in hand, the solution may become easier. A change in medication can help reduce problematic side effects or significantly lower cost. Physical activity recommendations can be modified to fit the realities of the patient’s life. Dietary guidance can be adjusted to align with the patient’s finances, access, and culture. In other cases, understanding the “why” may lead to addressing depression, anxiety, challenging family dynamics, or long-standing, habitual behaviors that interfere with compliance.

This is why integrated care is critical and where it can make a profound difference. When the patient’s primary care provider is attuned and healthcare teams work together, we change the course of treatment. It all starts with changing the questions we ask, moving from “What should the patient do to get better?” to “What is going to help this patient do the things needed to get better?” This way, we help close the gap between knowing what to do and getting it done.

item.title: From Connection to No Contact: The Continuum of Estrangement
item.description:
Family Dynamics

From Connection to No Contact: The Continuum of Estrangement

The spectrum of family emotional and physical distancing.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Family estrangement can be a long and difficult process.
  • Estrangement is a continuum that ranges from growing distance to complete dissolution.
  • Distance is not a punishment but a way to protect your well-being.

People tend to imagine family relationships in binaries:

You either have a relationship with your mother or you don't.

You're either close to your family or estranged from them.

In reality, relational distance exists on a continuum.

Family estrangement is often portrayed as a dramatic, impulsive moment when someone “cuts off” a relative. In truth, it is often a slow and difficult process that follows years and even decades of chronic boundary violations, continued emotional harm, refusal of accountability, and unsuccessful attempts to repair.

Estrangement as a Continuum

A useful way to conceptualize estrangement is as a continuum that ranges from growing emotional distance to the complete dissolution of the relationship.

Source: AI Generated

Stage 1: Cordial Contact

In this early stage, the relationship remains outwardly intact. Inwardly, however, something has shifted.

A person may begin paying closer attention to how they feel before, during, and after interactions. Past experiences may be reconsidered, and behaviors that were once normalized may begin to feel unhealthy, hurtful, or incompatible with the relationship they want.

This stage can involve considerable ambivalence. The person may still want the relationship but begin questioning whether it can continue in its current form.

They may also attempt repair by expressing concerns, asking for different treatment, or communicating new boundaries.

Stage 2: Low Contact

If concerns persist, the individual may deliberately reduce the relative's access.

This might include calling less often, shortening visits, declining some family events, and limiting certain topics.

The reduction in contact may bring conflicting emotions. There can be guilt, sadness, anger, uncertainty, and anxiety—but also relief.

Distance sometimes gives people enough psychological space to evaluate the relationship without the constant influence of family expectations, criticism, or pressure.

Importantly, low contact does not necessarily mean that the person has decided to end the relationship. It may instead represent an attempt to determine whether the relationship can function with stronger boundaries.

This phase can also create an opportunity for the other family member to listen, reflect, acknowledge their contribution to the conflict, and demonstrate meaningful behavioral change.

Stage 3: No Contact

This is where most people mistakenly believe that estrangement begins. However, no contact occurs when communication stops for a period of time.

The individual no longer initiates or accepts contact. This may last weeks, months, years, or indefinitely.

However, no contact and complete estrangement are not necessarily the same thing.

A person can stop communicating with a family member while still psychologically considering that person part of their family.

For example, siblings may stop speaking after a serious conflict but still imagine that a relationship could someday be restored.

No contact can therefore represent a boundary or period of separation without necessarily representing the complete emotional end of the relationship.

Stage 4: Complete Estrangement

At the far end of the continuum is complete estrangement. This is rare. Most people will reconcile after a period of no contact.

In estrangement, the individual no longer experiences the relative as someone with whom they have an active family relationship.

The relationship is severed completely, but the important distinction is emotional disengagement.

Individuals may take practical steps to prevent future contact such as blocking telephone and social media communication and notifying other relatives not to share information with the estranged individual.

The disconnect may occur with or without the estranged relative being informed or included in the decision.

No Contact vs. Estrangement

No contact and estrangement are not the same. No contact describes communication. Complete estrangement describes the perceived relationship itself.

A person who is not speaking to a sibling may still think, "that is my brother, and someday we might repair this."

A completely estranged person may instead experience the relationship as something that has ended.

That ending can still involve grief. Emotional separation does not necessarily mean indifference; someone may mourn the loss of the relationship while also believing that remaining disconnected is necessary for their well-being.

The Continuum Is Not Necessarily Linear

People do not necessarily move neatly from cordial contact → low contact → no contact → complete estrangement.

Someone may move from low contact back to greater connection. They may attempt to reconcile after years of no contact. They may resume limited contact following a major life event or return to no contact after another serious boundary violation.

This process is better understood as a changing level of relational access than as a permanent state.

Family estrangement, most often, reflects an evolving process of deciding how much access a difficult family relationship can safely have to your life. For some, that means stronger boundaries or less frequent contact. For others, it means no contact or the end of the relationship altogether. The goal is not necessarily distance for its own sake, but finding the level of connection, or separation, that best protects your well-being.

item.title: A Nation's Shame, a Family's Tragedy
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

A Nation's Shame, a Family's Tragedy

Proof that America's mental health system is broken.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Lindsay Clancy faces first-degree murder charges while allegedly suffering postpartum psychosis.
  • Postpartum psychosis is rare but treatable — the system meant to catch it failed Clancy repeatedly.
  • A comparison to the case of Andrea Yates demonstrates that courts often lag behind clinical reality.
  • That mental health care remains underfunded and inaccessible is a policy choice, not a scientific limitation.

Three children are dead. Cora was five. Dawson was three. Callan was eight months old. Their mother killed them. Their mother was sick, and everyone who should have stopped it knew she was sick.

If further evidence were needed that America's mental health system is broken, the trial now underway in Plymouth Superior Court settles it.

Lindsay Clancy, a 36-year-old labor and delivery nurse, is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children on January 24, 2023. She has pleaded not guilty. Her attorney does not dispute that she killed them; he argues she was not criminally responsible — but in the grip of postpartum psychosis, destabilized by a rapid succession of medications, and failed by the system meant to treat her. Prosecutors say she acted rationally. She attends court in a wheelchair, paralyzed by a fall from a window that same night — an attempt to end her own life.

I have spent four decades as a practicing psychiatrist, seventeen years chairing one of the country's largest and leading academic departments, and a term as president of the American Psychiatric Association. I side with the defense.

But the jury's question is not the country's. The one it will never be asked is this: How does a young woman with a recognized, treatable illness — insured, working in health care herself, married to an attentive husband, actively asking for help — end up here?

She got there because we let her. Americans have historically practiced discrimination by race, sex, religion, and disability, but in time we softened and even overcame these prejudices. People with serious mental illness are the conspicuous exception. Their care is not accessible, not affordable, and nowhere near commensurate with what we know about brain disorders and how well our treatments work. That gap is not a scientific problem. It is a choice, renewed annually in budgets and benefit designs — and it constitutes a civil rights failure.

A condition we understand well and treat badly

Nothing in Lindsay’s case is mysterious. The "baby blues" affect half to 75 percent of new mothers. Perinatal depression, a disorder requiring treatment, affects one in seven. Postpartum psychosis, the severest form, strikes one to two of every thousand deliveries — or several thousand American women a year.

Rare is not unpredictable. It announces itself early, and it carries identifiable risk factors. Given its association with suicide and, in a fraction of cases, infanticide, it is one of psychiatry's few true emergencies. And it responds to treatment. It is precisely what a functioning system is built to catch.

Testimony in Lindsay’s trial described medications started, stopped, combined, and changed repeatedly over a short span; contact conducted largely by phone or portal; a patient reporting that nothing was working. What any clinician did is the court's business, not mine. I am certain only of this: Her illness was treatable and this outcome preventable. Nor is the pattern aberrant. It is what today’s community care looks like — clinicians working alone, without a bed to admit to, without a day program with an opening, without a reproductive psychiatrist for a hundred miles.

The result is not negligence by any one hand. It is abandonment by design.

Screening with nowhere for people to go

Source: Варвара Курочкина / Pexels

The obvious remedy is screening built into obstetric care, and on paper we have it. The failure is downstream. A positive screen means nothing unless it guarantees treatment, and too many American women get a phone number instead. Obstetricians get the questionnaire but not the training to read an evolving mental status, not the time to draw out symptoms a frightened mother is ashamed to volunteer, not a referral network with an appointment this month. Screening without capacity only manufactures reassurance.

We know what works: training that distinguishes ordinary distress from a gathering psychosis; behavioral health embedded in obstetric practice; insurance that covers psychiatric care; access programs that put a psychiatrist on the phone the same day. None of it is speculative. It exists elsewhere. We decline to pay.

The lesson we should have learned

In June 2001, Andrea Yates drowned her five children in her Houston bathtub, in the grip of postpartum psychosis and the delusion that she was saving them from damnation. Convicted of capital murder in 2002, she won reversal in 2005; a second jury found her not guilty by reason of insanity in 2006. Yates is proof the system needed five years and two juries to reach what every treating psychiatrist saw immediately.

Such cases reach the public because they are sensational. They are the visible tip of an enormous mass of avoidable suffering: mothers who cannot bond with their infants, who become incapacitated, who hide intrusive thoughts of harm because they correctly fear what disclosure will cost them. In a New Jersey case that was recently resolved, the court sent a defendant found not guilty by reason of insanity to a private hospital her family paid for out of pocket rather than a state facility resembling a prison. That the line dividing treatment from imprisonment ran through a bank account is unacceptable.

The stepchild of medicine

Psychiatry remains the only medical specialty with an organized movement opposed to its existence. We have a substantial evidence base and effective treatments. What we lack are objective diagnostic tests, and that absence invites the suspicion that mental disorders are normal behavior pathologized. Patients pay for it in denied care.

The mechanisms for this predicament are fixable. Hospitals devote a sliver of their budgets to behavioral health, and psychiatric beds are the first cut when margins tighten. Coverage remains inferior to that for every other organ system. Former Congressman Patrick Kennedy won federal parity legislation for mental health care in 2008, but enforcement is still weak enough that narrow networks and denied authorizations accomplish quietly what the law forbids.

Most damning is how little has changed. From antiquity till the present, society has had two responses to the mentally ill: cast them out or lock them up. The homeless of American cities are the successors of those who once wandered the countryside; jails and state hospitals have replaced the poor and almshouses. We changed the architecture and kept the practice.

Whatever the jury decides, Lindsay Clancy is an emblem of that cruelty. Three children are dead who did not have to die. Perhaps their deaths will bring us to a tipping point — one at which our government and our health care system are finally obliged to treat the brain as they treat the rest of the body.

item.title: The Medical Model in American Psychoanalysis
item.description:
Psychoanalysis

The Medical Model in American Psychoanalysis

A tradition rooted in both careful description and psychodynamic understanding.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • American psychoanalysis developed a strong tradition linking diagnosis with psychodynamic understanding.
  • The medical model need not reduce mental disorders to biology or exclude psychological meaning.
  • Grinker, Gunderson, and modern psychodynamic psychiatry show that diagnosis and depth can coexist.

Psychoanalysis is sometimes portrayed as standing in opposition to the medical model of mental illness. According to this familiar account, psychiatry concerns itself with diagnosis, classification, and disease, while psychoanalysis is interested in meaning, conflict, development, and the individual person.

There is some historical basis for this distinction, but it overlooks an important tradition within American psychoanalysis: one that regarded psychoanalytic understanding and the medical model not as competitors but as complementary approaches to psychopathology.

(Medical model in this context does not imply that psychiatric conditions are reducible to biological abnormalities, but rather that they can be studied as clinically recognizable syndromes with characteristic features, courses, prognoses, and responses to treatment.)

This tradition became closely associated with what is now called psychodynamic psychiatry. Its practitioners were psychoanalysts and psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapists, but their interests extended well beyond psychoanalytic treatment or theory narrowly conceived. They studied psychiatric syndromes, diagnosis, personality, developmental psychopathology, and treatment. The question was not whether a patient should be understood diagnostically or dynamically, but what could be learned from each level of understanding.

American psychoanalysis developed in particularly close proximity to medicine and psychiatry. Unlike psychoanalysis in most other parts of the world, where nonmedical or "lay" analysis became firmly established, organized American psychoanalysis historically maintained close ties to academic medicine. For much of the mid-twentieth century, psychoanalysts occupied prominent positions in American medical schools and departments of psychiatry.

Roy R. Grinker Sr., M.D. (1900–1993), a champion of diagnosis and scientific inquiry in American psychoanalysis.
Source: Psychology Today

Undoubtedly, this arrangement had its problems. At the height of psychoanalytic influence, dynamic explanations often displaced rather than supplemented traditional descriptive psychopathology, and psychiatric syndromes were interpreted primarily in terms of presumed underlying conflicts. But another strand of American psychoanalysis took a different path. It attempted to bring psychoanalytic ideas into dialogue with systematic observation, diagnosis, and eventually empirical research.

Roy R. Grinker Sr. was representative of this orientation. A psychiatrist and psychoanalyst at the University of Chicago, Grinker was deeply interested in psychoanalytic ideas but skeptical of psychoanalytic dogmatism. His work attempted to bring dynamic understanding into contact with careful clinical description and scientific investigation. (For a wonderful tribute to Grinker, see this Psychology Today piece by Paul C. Hollinger, M.D.)

In The Borderline Syndrome, published with Beatrice Werble and Robert C. Drye in 1968, Grinker made the point explicitly:

The unpopularity of diagnosis and knowledge of the life history of describable entities is a reaction against the 'disease' concept in psychiatry and over emphasis on individual dynamic processes. Yet the pendulum has swung too far in the direction of concern only with 'the problem' of a specific patient. (Grinker et al., 1968, p. v)

For Grinker, classification was not the enemy of psychological understanding but a prerequisite for scientific inquiry. As he and his colleagues put it elsewhere in the same volume, "No science can exist without a foundation of description and classification of its subject matter as the 'what' of study" (p. 7). Science could then proceed beyond description toward questions of how and why—precisely the kinds of questions to which psychodynamic thinking might contribute.

John Gunderson continued this tradition in his work on borderline psychopathology. Although psychoanalytically trained, Gunderson did not simply elaborate another theory of "borderline personality." Beginning in the 1970s, he sought to determine whether borderline patients could be reliably identified and distinguished from patients with other psychiatric conditions (Gunderson & Singer, 1975). His early work helped move borderline psychopathology from a loosely defined psychoanalytic concept toward an empirically investigable psychiatric syndrome.

Yet, Gunderson never abandoned psychological understanding. Rather, he helped establish a diagnosis that could first be described and studied and then psychologically explained. In his 1984 textbook, he outlined a specific theory of borderline personality disorder (BPD) based on ego psychology; it now forms the basis for Good Psychiatric Management, an empirically supported treatment for BPD. Diagnosis, in Grinker's and Gunderson's conception, does not replace psychodynamics. The two inform each other.

This orientation continues in contemporary psychodynamic psychiatry. Richard Friedman, Jennifer Downey, and César Alfonso have argued that modern psychodynamic psychiatry should no longer be regarded simply as a "child" of psychoanalysis. They describe it instead as an emerging discipline drawing simultaneously from psychoanalytic psychology, neuroscience, academic psychiatry, developmental science, and research outside psychoanalysis (Friedman et al., 2014).

Importantly, this approach does not assume that psychoanalytic theory possesses a privileged route to truth about the mind. Friedman and colleagues explicitly describe contemporary psychodynamic psychiatry as favorable toward empirical research, neuroscience and psychobiology, academic psychology, psychopharmacology, and descriptive psychiatry. At the same time, it retains ideas that emerged from psychoanalysis—most importantly, the notion that much mental life is unconscious, motivated, and psychologically meaningful.

Their position on diagnosis is particularly relevant. Descriptive psychopathology tells us about recognizable patterns of illness, their epidemiology, course, and clinical presentation. Psychodynamic assessment adds the patient's developmental and autobiographical history—the personal narrative through which a condition takes shape in an individual's life. Neither alone provides the whole picture.

This also means that a medically oriented psychodynamic approach places diagnostic assessment before allegiance to any particular treatment. Not every patient whose issues can be understood psychodynamically requires psychoanalysis or long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy. Some require medication, supportive treatment, structured psychotherapy, environmental intervention, or combinations of these approaches. Furthermore, some problems in psychiatry do not necesarilly lend themselves to psychodynamic understanding. The medical model, properly understood, begins with the condition of the patient rather than the preferred treatment of the clinician. In this sense, it avoids psychoanalytic dogmatism.

This American psychoanalytic tradition differs somewhat from major strands of psychoanalysis elsewhere in the world. Freud himself famously defended lay analysis and resisted reducing psychoanalysis to a medical specialty, even though he favored a scientific approach and valued basic diagnostic distinctions. In Britain, France, Latin America, and elsewhere, psychoanalysis often developed with considerably greater intellectual and institutional independence from academic psychiatry. Distinct theoretical schools—Kleinian, Lacanian, Winnicottian, and others—also became important sources of psychoanalytic identity.

American psychoanalysis certainly developed theoretical schools of its own, and it would be misleading to treat it as uniformly medical or empirical. But its unusually intimate historical relationship with psychiatry created another possibility: the psychoanalyst as psychopathologist, interested not only in the unconscious meanings of symptoms but also in defining, differentiating, and studying the conditions in which those symptoms occur.

In my recent paper, "Psychiatric Diagnosis in Psychoanalysis: Integrating Nosology and Psychology," published in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, I argued for recovering this distinction. Diagnosis and psychoanalytic formulation answer fundamentally different questions. Diagnosis asks what disorder or syndrome a patient has; psychoanalytic formulation asks why the condition takes the particular psychological form it does in this particular person.

Importantly, defending diagnosis is not the same thing as defending every category in the DSM. Psychiatric diagnoses must themselves be evaluated on the basis of their validity or truthfulness (Robins & Guze, 1970). Some are much better established than others. The point is more basic: systematic description, differentiation, and validation of recurring forms of mental disorder remain essential tasks for psychiatry.

Modern discussions often imply that clinicians must choose between diagnosis and individuality, medicine and meaning, or science and psychological depth. Yet the American psychoanalytic tradition represented by Grinker and Gunderson, carried forward in different ways by Kernberg's transference-focused psychotherapy and contemporary psychodynamic psychiatry, suggests that these are false dichotomies.

We can classify illness without reducing people to these classifications. We can study psychiatric conditions scientifically without assuming that biology tells us the whole story. And we can search for unconscious meaning without abandoning the careful study of psychopathology.

This tradition is not merely of historical interest. I would argue that psychiatry is still very much in need of it.

item.title: How Listening Helps Build a Shared Reality
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

How Listening Helps Build a Shared Reality

Frameworks for navigating conflicting viewpoints productively.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • People can enter a conversation with different versions of reality.
  • Disagreement often reflects different realities, not simply right versus wrong.
  • Shared reality grows when people listen for what they do not know.

Most of us know the feeling.

Someone at work sees the situation one way, and you see it another. Maybe they are more optimistic than you are. Maybe they are moving faster than you think is wise. Maybe you see risks or constraints they do not.

Do you speak up? Hold back? Try to persuade them?

Imagine the person is your manager.

Your manager tells you, “We need 12% growth next year. With AI helping sales and marketing become more productive, we can get there.”

You see a different picture. From where you sit, 6% to 8% looks more realistic. Your manager sees market opportunity and what AI might make possible. You are closer to customers, capacity constraints, and what the team can deliver today.

You are looking at the same situation and seeing something different.

The Reality Delta

In an earlier Psychology Today article, I introduced the "Reality Delta": the gap between what one person assumes and what another person sees or experiences from where they sit.

Reality deltas are common at work. A leader sees opportunity while someone closer to the work sees obstacles. A manager sees urgency while an employee sees the cost of moving too quickly.

The mistake is assuming that if our views differ, one of us must be seeing reality correctly.

Often, each person is seeing only part of the picture.

Psychologist E. Tory Higgins and his colleagues use the term "shared reality" to describe something deeper than agreement. Shared reality involves a sense of commonality in how people understand or relate to something in the world. It helps us connect with others and make sense of what is happening around us (Higgins et al., 2021).

Shared reality does not require seeing everything the same way. It means understanding enough of what the other person sees that the picture becomes fuller for both of you.

For leaders, this matters. The higher you rise, the easier it is to become separated from the realities others experience. Building shared reality can help leaders make better judgments and make it safer for people to say, “I see it differently.”

How do we narrow the reality delta and build more shared reality?

It starts with listening.

Listening Helps Us See More

Listening sounds simple until we strongly disagree.

In our review of listening in organizations, Colin Fisher and I identified a listening paradox. Being listened to can be highly beneficial for the speaker, while genuine listening requires effort from the listener (Yip & Fisher, 2022).

Disagreement makes that effort harder. When someone challenges our judgment, we start preparing our response while they are still talking. We listen for the flaw or the opening that will help us make our case.

Research by Guy Itzchakov and colleagues shows what can happen when people listen differently. Across four experiments involving disagreement, high-quality listening increased speakers’ sense of connection and encouraged less defensive reflection on their own attitudes. These processes were associated with lower polarization (Itzchakov et al., 2024).

Listening does not require agreement. It gives us a chance to see something we could not see from our own vantage point.

Instead of telling your manager, “12% is unrealistic,” you ask:

“What are you seeing that makes 12% feel achievable?”

Your manager explains that some teams are already using AI to prepare for client meetings much faster and expects those capabilities to improve.

Now you understand something new. The 12% figure includes an assumption about future capability, not just current performance.

You may still disagree, but you now share more of the reality than you did before.

That is the foundation for a REAL conversation.

A REAL Conversation

REAL offers four moves for thinking something through together:

Recognize what matters. Exchange perspectives. Ask to expand possibilities. Land with clear direction.

Real Conversations framework
Source: Jeffrey Yip

R: Recognize what matters

Before debating the number, start with what matters.

“I agree that growth matters and that we should be getting more value from AI. I want us to find the strongest path to get there.”

You have not agreed to 12%. You have recognized what sits underneath the position.

This matters because we often argue over positions before understanding the priorities behind them. Starting with what matters gives the conversation somewhere more useful to begin.

E: Exchange perspectives

Share what you see, then inquire into what the other person sees.

“Based on the current pipeline and our capacity, I think we’re closer to 6% to 8%. AI is helping, but we’re not yet seeing gains that support 12%. What are you seeing that I may be missing?”

The goal is not simply to exchange opinions. It is to understand the evidence, experiences, and assumptions behind each perspective.

Stay close to what is observable before jumping to interpretation.

A useful test is: Did I learn something I did not know before?

If not, you may have exchanged views without really expanding the reality you share.

A: Ask to expand possibilities

Once you can see more, resist the urge to compromise too quickly.

Your manager says 12%. You say 6% to 8%. Settling at 9% may resolve the disagreement, but it does not necessarily improve the plan.

Instead ask:

“What would have to be true for us to get closer to 12%?”

The question neither accepts nor dismisses the target. It opens it up.

Recent research on integrative negotiation finds that open-ended questions can elicit more information and contribute to greater value creation (Di Stasi et al., in press).

The conversation shifts from “Is 12% realistic?” to “What could change what is possible?”

Perhaps more focused AI use and added capacity could make 9% to 10% plausible. If those changes strengthen the pipeline, 12% might remain a stretch possibility.

L: Land with clear direction

Clear direction does not always mean a final decision. It might be an experiment, something to investigate, or a point when you will revisit the issue.

You might agree to work toward 9%, focus AI where it is producing the strongest gains, add capacity, and review the evidence in three months.

You do not need complete agreement.

A good conversation should leave you clearer about what you understand, what remains uncertain, and where to go next.

Real conversations at work
Source: Jeffrey Yip

When You See It Differently

REAL Conversations can help with disagreement, coaching, feedback, and problem-solving.

The goal is not to make differences disappear. It is to take seriously the possibility that another person sees something you do not.

item.title: Helping Your Teen Survive Their First Heartbreak
item.description:
Parenting

Helping Your Teen Survive Their First Heartbreak

Recognizing what you can do to help and what you can't.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • A teen's first heartbreak can be emotionally overwhelming.
  • The grief and trauma caused by a first breakup can have long-lasting effects.
  • Parents who can empathize and relate to their teen's pain can be more effective in helping them.

One of the hardest things for teens to deal with is their first heartbreak. As they reach puberty and start to have sexual feelings, who they choose has a lot to do with how they feel about themselves. Teens who feel secure may pick someone who also feels good about themselves. This may lead to mutual respect and treating each other well. On the other hand, teens who are down on themselves, who don’t recognize their value, and who may feel not worth being loved by someone, may choose a relationship partner more poorly.

When someone believes they are worthwhile, then they’re most likely going to expect that the person they become involved with will treat them well. Teens who feel bad about themselves and unlovable may feel lucky that anyone would want to be with them. This makes them more likely to connect with other people who are down on themselves, or worse yet, people with predatory inclinations.

Adults Have Perspective That Teens May Lack

Adults may know that people tend to go through a number of relationships in their lives. Teens may not know this. For a teen, first love may seem like a magical time that’s going to last forever. That’s why their first breakup can be such a soul-crushing experience. The wounds that teens experience when their first love falls apart may be wounds that take them years, if not decades, to get over.

For example, if a teen is cheated on by someone they are in a relationship with, the cause may be as simple as the other person is young and doesn’t yet understand the importance of commitment. People learn as they go and often can be tempted by someone else if they are solely guided by their feelings and not thinking about their commitment. Of course, when this happens, it can cause great pain to the person who is caught by surprise by their actions.

When someone is cheated on, they often don't see it coming and it completely alters their sense of what’s real in their life. This can trigger their biggest fears about themselves. Inadvertently, the person who cheated on them may be confirming their partner's fears of not being good enough; or not worthy of love; or that people can’t be trusted. This can then play into their future relationships, where the person who was wounded in this way may distrust the next person they start a relationship with and stay suspicious throughout their time together. These feelings may cause them to continually check up on the person and want to control who they communicate with in their lives. Needless to say this can make their new relationship partner feel distrusted, or emotionally suffocated. Then, when the relationship ends, the sad truth is that it ended because of previous hurt and was not about the current relationship at all. This is just one example of a the dangers of previous trauma affecting current relationships. The question then becomes, what can be done about it?

How Can Parents Help?

The bottom line is that it's very difficult for parents to get through to their teen when their child is in the midst of a breakup. Their feelings can be overwhelming, and all the logic in the world is not going to dampen their intense grief and pain. The best thing parents can do is to try to align themselves with their teen. Take a minute to remember your own first breakup and the pain you felt. This will make it easier to relate to what your teen is going through. Try to empathize and be extra supportive. You can do your best to help build up your child’s confidence and value. This is not about idly praising them; it’s about letting them know that this difficult time doesn’t diminish who they are as a person. By letting them know they deserve to be loved and cared for, parents can help build up a child’s self-confidence to give them more emotional strength to deal with the situation.

When a child is going through a breakup, it can feel like the end of the world. As a parent, it may not seem as big a deal as it does to your child. The best way to help them is to recognize that this is one of the most traumatic experiences your child has faced in their young life. You may know that they are going to find other people to care about in the future. At this time, they do not. To them, this is almost like a death. They likely do not have the perspective to realize that this is the first of a number of relationships they’ll have in their lives. To them, it’s soul-crushing and one of the worst things they’ve ever experienced. By understanding their pain, you can help them see they are not alone. When teens feel their parents understand their pain, it helps to build trust.

Final Thoughts

A teen’s first breakup can be heartbreaking. They most likely don’t have perspective on the situation, and nothing you say is going to make it better at that moment. They need time to heal, to mentally recover from the emotional severity of their loss. By not dismissing their pain, but instead showing empathy and caring, you can provide a safe place for your teen.

Of course, if your child’s emotional distress is causing them to threaten to take dangerous actions or harm themselves, it’s important to take those situations seriously and get them the help they need. The bottom line is that if your child is in emotional pain and struggling with the heartbreak of the loss of first love, your understanding and support can make a big difference in helping them work through the emotional pain they are feeling.
